sections.h2: The Ridgewood certificate you need before closing
sections.html:
Before closing, a Ridgewood seller must hold a smoke detector and carbon monoxide certificate from the Fire Prevention Bureau. The village Building Department issues no certificate of occupancy when a one or two family house is resold, so this one inspection is the main local hurdle.

Ridgewood is a Bergen County village about 20 miles northwest of Midtown Manhattan, with an estimated 26,527 residents in July 2025 and 8,903 households. Of occupied homes, 82.5 percent are owner-occupied, the middle home value is $891,200 and median household income is $208,211. Most sales are family houses changing hands, and the price puts a typical sale in the top band of the state transfer fee schedule, covered below.

The fee depends on how far ahead of closing you book. The bureau charges per dwelling unit and takes appointments on weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. through the Inspection Office at 201-444-7898, extension 5480.

Fire Prevention Bureau resale inspection fees
When you bookFee per dwelling unit
More than 10 days before closing$120
Fewer than 10 days before closing$150
Within 3 days of closing$200
Inspection done after closing$200 plus a $500 penalty

State law requires the certificate before transfer, which is why a late visit carries the penalty. Settle the fee at the bureau, 201 East Glen Avenue, with cash or a check made out to the Village of Ridgewood. Cards are taken in person only and add a 3 percent technology charge.

If the house has a monitored central station alarm, register it with the Ridgewood Fire Department at 201-444-8822, extension 4112.

sections.h2: Permits that can slow a Ridgewood closing
sections.html:
The village building FAQ lists work that needs a permit: replacing a furnace, boiler or water heater, creating habitable space in a basement or attic, adding a bathroom or laundry room, and building a deck, generator pad or accessory structure. Pools, patios, driveways, sheds and fences need a zoning certificate first.

Painting, flooring, trim, and replacing a window or door in the same opening need no permit. A permit lapses if work has not begun within 12 months, or if work stops for 6 months.

  • Cutting a tree with a trunk eight inches or wider at breast height on private land takes a permit. Trees in the public right-of-way belong to the village.
  • Sidewalk repair is the owner's job, and the village arborist assesses any shade tree whose roots lift the slab.
  • New Jersey allows an oil tank to be abandoned in place with a permit, though lenders and insurers increasingly want a buried tank removed, and that can come up at sale.

Several Dutch-era homes in Ridgewood are on the National Register of Historic Places, among them the Ackerman houses on Doremus Avenue and Lincoln Avenue, the Archibald-Vroom House at 160 East Ridgewood Avenue and the Westervelt-Cameron House on East Glen Avenue.

The Historic Preservation Commission may review exterior changes. If you own an older house, ask the Building Department whether any approval applies before you advertise a renovation or addition as a selling point.

sections.h2: What to do if the inspection fails
sections.html:
Most failed visits come down to a missing or dead detector. Replace the device, then call the Inspection Office to book the follow-up. The fee climbs as the closing date nears, so the cheapest path is to call the week you list or sign, not the week you close.

  • Have every detector in place and working before the inspector arrives.
  • Put carbon monoxide protection where the code calls for it, and test each unit.
  • If the house has a monitored alarm, confirm the registration with the fire department.
  • Keep the certificate with your closing papers and hand a copy to your attorney.

A buyer paying cash can close quickly, but the same certificate is still needed, so a cash sale does not remove this step.

sections.h2: From contract to closing in the village
sections.html:
The local sequence is short, and following it in order keeps the fee at the low end.

  1. Call the Inspection Office as soon as the contract is signed and ask for the earliest weekday slot.
  2. Walk the house first. Check each detector, and look at any alarm panel for trouble signals.
  3. Bring payment to 201 East Glen Avenue, by check or cash if you want to avoid the card charge.
  4. Pass the inspection and keep the certificate with the file your attorney holds for closing.
  5. Close with the seller's transfer fee and any tax adjustments on the settlement statement.

Because Ridgewood houses are often older, a buyer's inspector may find more than the village does. Fixing small items before the village visit saves a second trip and keeps the buyer's repair requests short.

sections.h2: Buried oil tanks and older systems
sections.html:
Many Ridgewood houses carry an old heating system, and some still sit over a buried oil tank. The state permits a tank to be closed in place under a permit, yet buyers' lenders and insurers have been leaning toward full removal. If you know a tank is underground, gather whatever paperwork exists about its closure and bring it up with your attorney before the first showing.

Replacing a furnace, boiler or water heater needs a village permit, so a seller who swapped one without a permit should talk to the Building Department before the buyer's inspector spots it. Closing the permit properly is quicker than explaining a gap after an offer is in.

Bergen County takes assessment appeals through its Board of Taxation at Two Bergen County Plaza in Hackensack, 201-336-6300. The annual filing date is April 1, and hearings follow later in the year. When an assessment tops $750,000, a Ridgewood owner may skip the county board and file directly with the Tax Court by April 1.

Gather recent sales of similar houses nearby before you file. If an appeal is pending when you sell, tell your attorney so the buyer hears about it before closing.

The seller pays New Jersey's Realty Transfer Fee when the deed is recorded. Each band of the state schedule applies only to the slice of price inside that band. At Ridgewood prices, a sale lands in the upper band of that schedule.

Above $1,000,000, a graduated percent fee also falls on the seller: 1 percent of the total price up to $2,000,000. Ask your closing attorney or title agent for the total before you set a bottom line on an offer, so the net you expect matches what the settlement statement shows.

faqs.q: Does Ridgewood issue a certificate of occupancy at resale?
faqs.a: No. The village Building Department does not issue one for the resale of a one or two family house. A smoke detector and carbon monoxide certification from the Fire Prevention Bureau is required before closing.

faqs.q: What happens if the Ridgewood inspection is done after closing?
faqs.a: The owner pays a $500 penalty on top of the $200 certification fee. The schedule is $120 more than 10 days out, $150 inside 10 days and $200 inside 3 days.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to remove a tree before selling in Ridgewood?
faqs.a: Yes for a qualifying tree, meaning one eight inches or wider at breast height on private land. Trees in the public right-of-way need consent from the village arborist.

faqs.q: Is a Ridgewood buyer likely to ask about water quality?
faqs.a: Some will. Ridgewood Water entered a consent order with the state in May 2023 to treat PFAS in its groundwater supply, with a stated goal of finishing treatment by the end of 2026. The utility publishes current test data.

faqs.q: How is the transfer fee handled on a Ridgewood sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays it when the deed is recorded, and sales over $1,000,000 add a percentage fee. Your closing attorney can give you the exact amount for your price.
